issues.legal_issue: A court assessing whether a signature on a sale agreement is genuine must not give a handwriting expert’s opinion precedence over credible substantive and corroborating evidence without adequate reason.
material_facts: The trial court found the plaintiff and two attesting witnesses credible; their evidence consistently supported execution of the sale agreement.
A receipt for earnest money connected with the agreement bore the alleged seller’s signature, and there was no reliable evidence that the money had not been received or a challenge to that signature.
The alleged seller’s brother identified the disputed signature and the seller’s admitted signature on a partition document as genuine.
The High Court rejected the witnesses on erroneous factual assumptions and relied solely on the handwriting expert’s opinion to find the agreement forged.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in preferring the expert’s opinion to the consistent witness testimony and corroborating transaction evidence. On the totality of the evidence, the disputed signature was genuine, and the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 45 and 46 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, expert opinion is relevant and open to challenge on facts, but it is generally a weak form of evidence and is not conclusive. A court must assess its reliability cautiously in light of all relevant evidence; corroboration may be sought as a matter of prudence, although it is not legally mandatory. Expert evidence should rarely take precedence over substantive evidence. The Court relied on Ram Chandra and Ram Bharosey v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1957 SC 381; Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, AIR 1964 SC 529; Magan Bihari Lal v. State of Punjab, (1977) 2 SCC 210; Murari Lal v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1980) 1 SCC 704; S. Gopal Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, (1996) 4 SCC 596; and Alamgir v. State (NCT, Delhi), (2003) 1 SCC 21.

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_specific_perfor: The proceeding is an appeal after a court dismissed a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.expert_opinion_is_sole_basis_for_rejecti: The court rejecting the signature relies solely on a handwriting expert’s opinion.
predicates.credible_attesting_witnesses_support_exe: The attesting witnesses give credible evidence supporting execution of the document.
predicates.transaction_evidence_corroborates_execut: Evidence connected with the transaction supports execution, such as a related receipt bearing the alleged signatory’s unchallenged signature.
predicates.familiar_witness_identifies_signature: A witness familiar with the alleged signatory’s handwriting identifies the disputed signature as that person’s.

issues.definition: When an appeal from dismissal of a specific-performance suit involves sole reliance on an expert opinion despite credible attesting witnesses, corroborating transaction evidence, and identification by a familiar witness, the disputed signature is treated as genuine and the expert opinion is not preferred.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s opinion identifying another person’s handwriting is relevant when the witness’s familiarity satisfies the statutory description of acquaintance, and its weight depends on the extent of that familiarity.
material_facts: The alleged signatory’s brother identified the disputed signature and an admitted signature on a partition document.

The brother and alleged signatory had lived in the same house for over three decades, and the brother had opportunities to observe the alleged signatory’s writing in the ordinary course of family affairs.
The brother’s identification and familiarity were not challenged in re-examination.
issues.conclusion: The brother was acquainted with the alleged signatory’s handwriting within the meaning of Section 47, and his testimony was relevant and could safely be relied on, with weight comparable to or greater than the expert evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes relevant the opinion of a person acquainted with another person’s handwriting. Its Explanation describes circumstances establishing acquaintance, including having seen the person write or having documents written by that person habitually submitted in the ordinary course of business. The weight of the opinion depends on the witness’s familiarity, including the frequency and recency of opportunities to observe and the witness’s power of observation.

predicates.witness_had_repeated_opportunities_to_ob: The witness had repeated opportunities to see that person write or otherwise become familiar with the person’s handwriting.
predicates.witness_familiarity_is_unchallenged: The opposing party does not challenge the witness’s claimed familiarity with the handwriting.

issues.definition: In a civil dispute about a signature, an identification by a witness with repeated, unchallenged opportunities to observe the handwriting is relevant and may be given weight comparable to expert opinion.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of the buyer’s signature on a sale agreement does not by itself invalidate the agreement when the seller signed it and the connected transaction evidence supports the agreement.
material_facts: The sale agreement was signed by the alleged seller and stated the property and consideration for the proposed sale.
A connected receipt evidenced payment of earnest money, bore the seller’s signature, and also bore the buyer’s signature.
The agreement and receipt formed part of the same transaction.
issues.conclusion: The absence of the buyer’s signature on the sale agreement did not invalidate the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the absence of the buyer’s signature does not ipso facto nullify an agreement where the seller’s signed document records the agreement to sell for consideration and a connected receipt evidences payment and receipt of earnest money. The Court treated the agreement and receipt as parts of the same transaction.

predicates.civil_dispute_over_sale_agreement: The proceeding concerns the validity or enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_signed_agreement_recording_sale_t: The seller signed a document recording the proposed sale and its terms.
predicates.connected_receipt_supports_transaction: A receipt connected with the agreement supports the transaction, including payment or receipt of earnest money.

issues.definition: A seller-signed agreement recording the sale terms is not invalidated merely because the buyer did not sign it when a connected receipt supports the transaction.

issues.legal_issue: An expert comparison based principally on admitted signatures created after the litigation began is unreliable as a basis for determining whether the disputed signature is genuine.
material_facts: The handwriting expert compared the disputed signature with several admitted signatures of the alleged signatory.
Except for a signature on a written statement in an earlier suit, the admitted signatures used for comparison were made after the present suit was filed.
The expert’s report did not account for the resulting concern about the validity of its comparison material.
issues.conclusion: The post-litigation signatures could not validly be used as comparison standards, and their use cast serious doubt on the reliability of the expert’s report, which could be discarded on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that admitted signatures made after the suit began could not serve as a valid basis for comparison in the circumstances of the case, and that relying on them cast serious doubt on the reliability of the expert report.

predicates.civil_signature_authenticity_dispute: The civil proceeding concerns whether a particular signature is genuine.
predicates.expert_comparison_uses_admitted_signatur: The expert uses admitted comparison signatures that were created after the litigation began.

issues.definition: In a civil signature dispute, an expert report relying on admitted comparison signatures created after litigation began is unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and establish readiness and willingness to perform the contract, but an additional oral demand need not be separately proved where the required pleading and evidence establish that demand and ability to perform.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s plaint specifically averred readiness and willingness to perform the contract and stated that the plaintiff had demanded receipt of the balance consideration and execution of a registered sale deed.
The plaintiff had sufficient funds to pay the balance consideration and the evidence satisfied the Court that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.
The High Court wrongly concluded that no evidence showed a demand for performance.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff had fulfilled the formalities required for specific performance and was ready and willing to perform; the High Court was wrong to find otherwise for want of proof of demand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, and Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, governs the pleadings and proof for a specific-performance suit. The claimant must plead and prove readiness and willingness. The Court observed that an oral demand cannot itself be proved by evidence, and found the required averments and evidence of financial ability and readiness in this case.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and claimant_pleads_readiness_and_willingness and claimant_pleads_demand_for_performance and evidence_shows_ability_to_pay_and_readiness

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.claimant_pleads_readiness_and_willingnes: The claimant expressly pleads readiness and willingness to perform the claimant’s contractual obligations.
predicates.claimant_pleads_demand_for_performance: The claimant pleads that performance was demanded from the other party.
predicates.evidence_shows_ability_to_pay_and_readin: The evidence establishes the claimant’s ability to pay the balance due and readiness to perform.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance proceeding, express pleadings of readiness, willingness, and demand, together with evidence of ability to pay and readiness to perform, satisfy the readiness-and-willingness requirement.
